cards.front: What does a driver license require of your health?
cards.back: Both physical and mental health shape how you drive, and a driver license requires that you be in good health.

cards.front: How can a cold, a headache or the flu affect your driving?
cards.back: Even a short illness such as a cold, a headache or the flu can leave you less alert and slower to respond behind the wheel.

cards.front: Why is even a brief nod-off at highway speed so dangerous?
cards.back: At fifty-five miles per hour a vehicle covers the length of a football field in three point seven seconds, so even a brief nod-off is dangerous.

cards.front: Where and when do drowsy-driving crashes happen most often?
cards.back: Crashes caused by drowsiness tend to be serious and happen most often on fast rural highways when the driver is traveling alone.

cards.front: What are the warning signs that you are getting drowsy behind the wheel?
cards.back: Signs of drowsiness include not remembering the last few miles, hitting a rumble strip or drifting out of your lane, yawning again and again, and struggling to focus or keep your eyes open.

cards.front: What should you do if you grow tired while driving, and how long do quick fixes help?
cards.back: If you grow tired while driving you should stop; a nap of fifteen to forty-five minutes and some caffeine help only for a while.

cards.front: How often should you take a break on a long drive, and what should you do?
cards.back: On a long drive, take a break at least every two hours: leave the car, stretch and walk briskly.

cards.front: What daily driving limit and medicine advice does the handbook give?
cards.back: The handbook suggests capping your driving at about three hundred to four hundred miles a day and avoiding medicines that make you drowsy.

cards.front: How is a nap with caffeine different from the regular long-trip break?
cards.back: A short nap with caffeine is only a temporary help for fatigue, while the long-trip habit is a stop at least every two hours.

cards.front: What is distracted driving?
cards.back: Distracted driving means any activity that might pull your attention away from the main job of driving.

cards.front: What are some common distractions behind the wheel?
cards.back: Common distractions include texting, phone use, eating or drinking, talking with passengers, grooming, reading maps, using navigation, watching video and adjusting audio equipment.

cards.front: How does distraction change a driver's reactions and awareness?
cards.back: Distracted drivers respond more slowly to events such as a car slowing to turn or pulling out of a side road, and they miss hazards like pedestrians or debris more often.

cards.front: Why do many distractions make it harder to avoid a crash?
cards.back: Many distractions make it harder to steer clear of a crash because they take at least one hand off the steering wheel.

cards.front: When does the handbook say a phone may be used while driving?
cards.back: Use a phone while driving only when truly necessary, for emergencies or to reach a parent, legal guardian or spouse, and only at a safe time and place.

cards.front: What phone habits does the handbook recommend for drivers?
cards.back: Let a passenger make the call for you, let unanswered calls go to a message, and secure the phone so it cannot fly around in a crash.

cards.front: What phone activity is unlawful for every North Carolina driver?
cards.back: North Carolina makes it unlawful to text or email on a cell phone while driving on a public street, highway or public vehicular area.

cards.front: What phone use is allowed for a driver under eighteen while the vehicle is moving?
cards.back: A driver under eighteen may not use a cell phone or related technology at all while the vehicle is moving, except to call nine hundred eleven in an emergency.

cards.front: How does the phone law for all drivers differ from the law for drivers under eighteen?
cards.back: Every driver is barred from texting or emailing while driving, but a driver under eighteen is barred from using a phone at all while moving, apart from a nine hundred eleven emergency call.

cards.front: What phone use is allowed while driving a school bus?
cards.back: No one may drive a school bus on a public road or vehicular area while using a cell phone or other mobile-device technology.

cards.front: Which phone rules are laws, and which are safety advice?
cards.back: The texting ban and the under-eighteen ban are laws, while advice to use a phone only for emergencies or family contact is a safety reminder rather than a separate legal rule.

cards.front: How should you handle a medicine that may affect your driving?
cards.back: Both prescription and over-the-counter medicines can affect driving, so learn how a medicine affects you and drive as little as possible while taking it.

cards.front: About what share of traffic deaths involve alcohol, according to the handbook?
cards.back: The handbook states that about thirty-eight percent of all traffic deaths involve alcohol.

cards.front: What kind of drug is alcohol, and what does it do to your reactions?
cards.back: Alcohol is a depressant that slows the brain, so you cannot respond, decide or react quickly.

cards.front: How does alcohol affect judgment of speed, distance and risk?
cards.back: Alcohol weakens your judgment of speed and of distance to other cars, people or objects, and gives false confidence that leads to bigger risks.

cards.front: How does alcohol affect handling several driving tasks at once?
cards.back: Alcohol makes it hard to handle more than one task, so while steering you may miss traffic lights, cars from side streets or pedestrians; it also upsets balance and causes sleepiness.

cards.front: What is the only thing that sobers a drinker?
cards.back: Only time sobers a drinker; coffee, a large meal or a cold shower will not.

cards.front: Can coffee, a big meal or a cold shower sober up a drinker?
cards.back: Coffee, a big meal and a cold shower do nothing to sober a drinker; only the passing of time does.

cards.front: What are some ways to avoid drinking and driving?
cards.back: Ways to avoid drinking and driving include planning a ride in advance, sharing a taxi, taking public transit, staying overnight with a friend, or riding with someone who has not been drinking.

cards.front: Over a lifetime of driving, what are the rough odds of a serious crash injury or death?
cards.back: Across a typical lifetime behind the wheel, the odds of a serious injury or death in a crash are roughly one in three.

cards.front: Who must wear a seat belt when a vehicle moves forward on a North Carolina road?
cards.back: In a vehicle built with seat belts, the driver and every passenger must wear a properly fastened belt whenever the vehicle moves forward on a North Carolina street or highway.

cards.front: Do air bags or automatic shoulder harnesses replace the need for a lap belt?
cards.back: Seat belts are still required in vehicles with air bags, and if the vehicle has automatic shoulder harnesses the lap belt must also be worn.

cards.front: If a vehicle has an automatic shoulder harness, is the lap belt still needed?
cards.back: Air bags never excuse the seat belt, and a vehicle with an automatic shoulder harness still requires the lap belt to be fastened.

cards.front: Which medical situation exempts an occupant from the seat belt law?
cards.back: The seat belt law exempts an occupant of a noncommercial vehicle whose medical or physical condition, or professionally certified phobia, prevents proper restraint.

cards.front: Which on-duty carriers are exempt from the seat belt law?
cards.back: Rural letter carriers of the Postal Service on duty and newspaper carriers delivering along their route are exempt from the seat belt law.

cards.front: When are frequent-stop delivery occupants exempt from wearing belts?
cards.back: Drivers or passengers who keep stopping to leave the vehicle or deliver items are exempt if the vehicle goes no faster than twenty miles per hour between stops.

cards.front: What speed limit keeps the frequent-delivery belt exemption valid?
cards.back: The frequent-delivery seat belt exemption applies only if the vehicle stays at or below twenty miles per hour between stops.

cards.front: Which farm, equipment and seating situations are exempt from the seat belt law?
cards.back: Other exemptions cover property-carrying vehicles used for farming within the state, vehicles not legally required to have belts, and situations where every belted or restraint-equipped seat is already taken.

cards.front: When are motor home occupants exempt from the seat belt law?
cards.back: In a motor home, occupants other than the driver and front-seat passengers are exempt when the motor home has at least four of the listed living facilities.

cards.front: How many unrestrained child deaths could correctly used safety seats prevent?
cards.back: Correctly used safety seats could save seven of every ten children who die while riding unrestrained.

cards.front: What makes a child safety seat the best choice, and where can families find low-cost seats?
cards.back: The best child seat is one used on every ride that fits your car and has a comfortable harness or shield, and low-cost rentals are often offered by local groups, hospitals and health departments.

cards.front: What must a driver do for every passenger under sixteen?
cards.back: A driver carrying any passenger under sixteen must make sure each one is secured in a child restraint or seat belt meeting the federal standards in force when it was made.

cards.front: What restraint must a child younger than eight and under eighty pounds use?
cards.back: A child younger than eight who weighs under eighty pounds must ride in a weight-appropriate child passenger restraint.

cards.front: When must a young child ride in the rear seat because of a front air bag?
cards.back: When a vehicle has an active front passenger air bag and a rear seat, a child under five weighing under forty pounds must ride in the rear unless the restraint is built for use with a front air bag.

cards.front: How do the under-eight rule and the rear-seat air bag rule differ in age and weight?
cards.back: A child under eight and under eighty pounds needs a weight-appropriate restraint, while the rear-seat rule near an active front air bag covers a child under five and under forty pounds.

cards.front: When may a child under eight weighing forty to eighty pounds use a lap belt alone?
cards.back: If no seat has a lap and shoulder belt for the restraint, a child under eight weighing forty to eighty pounds may ride with a properly fitted lap belt alone.

cards.front: What condition must be true before a lap belt alone is allowed for a young child?
cards.back: A lap belt alone is allowed for a child under eight weighing forty to eighty pounds only when no seat has a lap and shoulder belt for the restraint.

cards.front: How long should a child use a booster seat, and how should the adult belt fit?
cards.back: Children who have outgrown safety seats should use federally compliant booster seats until an adult belt fits: lap belt snug on the hips, not the stomach, and shoulder belt across the shoulder and chest, not the face or throat.

decks.module: Air bags, helmets and pickup beds

cards.front: How fast does an air bag deploy?
cards.back: An air bag bursts out of the dashboard at up to two hundred miles per hour, faster than an eye blink, so it is far from a soft pillow.

cards.front: Where should children twelve and younger ride?
cards.back: Children aged twelve and younger should ride buckled up in a rear seat.

cards.front: Where must a rear-facing infant never ride?
cards.back: An infant in a rear-facing safety seat must never ride in the front seat of a vehicle that has a passenger-side air bag.

cards.front: How should the lap and shoulder belts be positioned with air bags?
cards.back: Air bags only supplement belts: wear the lap belt under the abdomen and low on the hips, and the shoulder belt over the collarbone, away from the neck and across the breastbone.

cards.front: How far forward should the driver and front passenger seats be?
cards.back: Move the driver and front passenger seats as far back as practical, especially for shorter people.

cards.front: What helmet must motorcycle and moped riders and passengers wear?
cards.back: Every motorcycle or moped operator and passenger must wear a safety helmet meeting Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard two hundred eighteen.

cards.front: What marks a compliant motorcycle helmet?
cards.back: A compliant helmet has a firm polystyrene liner about one inch thick and a DOT symbol fixed permanently on the back by the maker; a sticker added later does not make it legal.

cards.front: Does adding a DOT sticker make a helmet compliant?
cards.back: A DOT symbol fixed permanently by the manufacturer marks a compliant helmet, while a DOT sticker sold separately or added by the rider does not.

cards.front: Who may not ride in the open bed of a pickup truck, and who is responsible?
cards.back: North Carolina bars children younger than sixteen from riding in the open bed of a pickup truck, and the driver is responsible for compliance, though the statute has some exemptions.

cards.front: How does the rear-seat age advice compare with the pickup bed law?
cards.back: Riding in the rear seat is advised for children twelve and under, while riding in an open pickup bed is prohibited by law for children under sixteen.

recap_hooks.text: A brief nod-off at highway speed covers a football field, so tired means stop.
Naps and caffeine help briefly; take a break every two hours.
Distraction is anything that pulls attention off driving and slows your reactions.
Use the phone only when truly necessary, and let a passenger call.
No texting for anyone, and no phone at all under eighteen.
No phone while driving a school bus.
Alcohol slows the brain and warps judgment.
Only time sobers, so plan a sober ride ahead.
Everyone buckles, and air bags never replace the belt.
Delivery stops are exempt only at twenty or slower between stops.
Every passenger under sixteen is restrained, and under eight and eighty means a child seat.
Under five and forty rides in back near an active front air bag.

recaps.module: Air bags, helmets and pickup beds

recap_hooks.text: Twelve and under in back, and never a rear-facing infant in front of an air bag.
Helmets need the maker's DOT symbol, and no children under sixteen in pickup beds.
